content.text: Students build on Investigation 1 by comparing progress inside the space program with slower change in schools and public life.
Scientific discovery grows through questions, evidence, and collaboration, but history also shows that social change does not always move at the same pace as scientific change.
Students will carry this skill of explaining connections between ideas into Chapter 20 and then into research on overlooked innovators.
Students will need to cite evidence to explain how an innovator’s work mattered and how barriers affected recognition of that work.

Directions:
Turn and talk with a partner to discuss your response to the following question.
In Chapter 18, the author shows that scientific progress in Virginia was moving quickly while social progress was moving slowly. What are some examples from the chapter that illustrate this contrast?
Language Study
This part of the lesson will help you to understand how an author uses figurative language to reveal central ideas.
Directions:

Look at this sentence from Chapter 18. We are going to study how the author uses figurative language to show an important idea in the chapter. As we discuss it, focus on what the words seem to mean on the surface and what they suggest at a deeper level.

“Virginia’s legacy as the birthplace of humanity’s first step into the heavens would have to compete with its embarrassing reputation as the country’s most outspoken opponent to the integration of public schools.”

This is a powerful sentence because the author uses figurative language to describe Virginia’s “legacy” as if it were something grand and historic—“the birthplace of humanity’s first step into the heavens.” At the same time, the author contrasts that imagery with details about Virginia’s real and painful history of resisting school integration. By placing these two ideas side by side, the author helps us see the tension between the state’s pride in its scientific achievements and the injustice created by segregation.
Turn and talk with a partner to respond to the following questions:
What is the literal, or surface‑level, meaning of the phrase “the birthplace of humanity’s first step into the heavens”?
When you look at the phrase figuratively, what deeper meaning do you notice?
Pulse Check
Which statement best explains how the figurative phrase “the birthplace of humanity’s first step into the heavens” functions in Chapter 18?
A. The author uses this phrase to convey the idea that people’s dreams can come true if they are determined and persevere.
B. The author uses figurative language to describe Virginia’s pride in being the place where scientists and mathematicians first made space travel possible.
C. The author uses this example of figurative language to describe the beauty of space as seen from Apollo 11.
D. The author uses this example of figurative language to describe the birthplace of the hidden innovators.
Part A: Understanding Technical Language
This part of the lesson will help you to identify technical vocabulary and understand how it supports key ideas in the chapter.
Review the following passage from Chapter 18.

“While the astronauts were preparing for this important mission, Katherine Goble had to calculate the flight trajectories. In other words, she had to plan the exact path that the spacecraft would travel across Earth’s surface, from the moment it lifted off the launch pad and flew through the atmosphere and into space, until it splashed back down in the Atlantic Ocean.” (pg. 150)

In this passage, the author uses technical vocabulary to explain the complex calculations Katherine had to complete. This explanation helps readers who may not have a scientific background understand challenging concepts. The passage includes words such as
calculate
trajectories
, and
atmosphere
, which help to highlight the key idea that Katherine had to determine the spacecraft’s precise path from launch to landing.
Directions:

Use the 3-Column Chart to identify examples of technical or domain-specific language from Chapter 18. Record your examples in the first column, what the language helps to explain in the second column, and how the word connects to a key idea in the text in the third column.
Label each column as indicated:
Column 1: Example of technical language
Column 2: What it explains
Column 3: Connection to a central idea
Part B: Analyzing the Development of a Central Idea

In Chapter 18, the author uses both figurative and technical language to reveal central ideas. The figurative phrase “the birthplace of humanity’s first step into the heavens” shows Virginia’s pride in its role in early space exploration, while also highlighting the contradiction that the state still enforced segregation and treated Black mathematicians and scientists unfairly. The technical terms—such as calculate, trajectories, and atmosphere—explain the precise, high‑stakes work Katherine was doing at the same time. Together, these language choices show that scientific progress was moving quickly, while social and legal progress lagged behind.
Quick Write
Directions:

Write a four‑to‑five‑sentence explanation of how the figurative phrase “the birthplace of humanity’s first step into the heavens” helps develop a central idea of Chapter 18. Use evidence from the text to support your response.
Reflection
Reflect on your ability to understand how figurative and technical language connects to central ideas using the Reflection routine.
How confident are you in your ability to explain how figurative and technical language can be used to convey a central idea?
Quick Write
Directions:

In three to four sentences, explain how the author uses both figurative language—such as the phrase “the birthplace of humanity’s first step into the heavens”—and technical language—such as the words calculate, trajectories, and atmosphere used to describe Katherine’s work—to convey central ideas in Chapter 18. Use details from the text to support your response.

This Turn and Talk helps students process key ideas about persistence, dedication, and collaboration in the Apollo 11 mission. It also prepares them for the upcoming analysis of how the author uses figurative language in the chapter.
Turn and Talk
Say these Directions:
Turn and talk with a partner to discuss your response to the following question.
Ask:
In Chapter 18, the author shows that scientific progress in Virginia was moving quickly while social progress was moving slowly. What are some examples from the chapter that illustrate this contrast?

One example of the contrast in Chapter 18 is that Virginia was proud to be the place where important scientific work for space travel was happening, including the calculations that helped launch humans into space. At the same time, the chapter explains that Virginia was still fighting against school integration and treating Black citizens unfairly. This shows that scientific progress was moving forward quickly, but social progress—like ending segregation—was moving much more slowly.
Connection to Today's Learning
Say:

Your partner discussion explored how Chapter 18 highlights two different speeds of progress: scientific progress moving forward quickly, while social progress moved slowly. This contrast is important to the chapter. Now we will look at how the author uses figurative language to help us understand this idea more deeply.
Activate prior learning from Chapter 17 and frame today’s work around unequal speeds of progress in science and society.

This part of the lesson helps students understand how figurative and literal language work together to reveal central ideas. Students examine how the author uses a symbolic description of Virginia’s legacy alongside factual details about segregation to highlight the contrast between the state’s pride in space exploration and its unfair treatment of Black citizens.
Language Study
Display the example of figurative language from Chapter 18 and read it aloud.

“Virginia’s legacy as the birthplace of humanity’s first step into the heavens would have to compete with its embarrassing reputation as the country’s most outspoken opponent to the integration of public schools.”
Say these Directions:

Look at this sentence from Chapter 18 as I read it aloud. We are going to study how the author uses figurative language to show an important idea in the chapter. As we discuss it, focus on what the words seem to mean on the surface and what they suggest at a deeper level.
Teach: Interpreting figurative language
Say:

This is a powerful sentence because the author uses figurative language to describe Virginia’s “legacy” as if it were something grand and historic—“the birthplace of humanity’s first step into the heavens.” At the same time, the author contrasts that imagery with details about Virginia’s real and painful history of resisting school integration. By placing these two ideas side by side, the author helps us see the tension between the state’s pride in its scientific achievements and the injustice created by segregation.
Prompt students to turn and talk with a partner to respond to the following questions:
Ask:
What is the literal, or surface‑level, meaning of the phrase “the birthplace of humanity’s first step into the heavens”?
If I look only at the surface meaning, it sounds like a place where humans literally took their first steps upward into the sky, almost like walking into the clouds.
Ask:
When you look at the phrase figuratively, what deeper meaning do you notice?

I think the phrase means that Virginia is proud to be the place where the scientific and mathematical work that made space travel possible first happened. It suggests that the state sees itself as the starting point for sending people into space.
Pulse Check (RI.6.4, L.6.5.a)
Which statement best explains how the figurative phrase “the birthplace of humanity’s first step into the heavens” functions in Chapter 18?
A. The author uses this phrase to convey the idea that people’s dreams can come true if they are determined and persevere.
Incorrect: This choice shifts the meaning toward a general motivational message rather than explaining how the phrase describes Virginia’s role in the space program.
B. The author uses figurative language to describe Virginia’s pride in being the place where scientists and mathematicians first made space travel possible.
Correct: This phrase highlights Virginia’s legacy as the starting point for the scientific work that led to human spaceflight.
C. The author uses this example of figurative language to describe the beauty of space as seen from Apollo 11.
Incorrect: This choice misinterprets the phrase as describing outer space itself, rather than Virginia’s symbolic role in launching the space program.
D. The author uses this example of figurative language to describe the birthplace of the hidden innovators.
Incorrect: This response narrows the meaning to the individuals (the “hidden” mathematicians) instead of the broader idea of Virginia as the symbolic starting point of human space exploration.
Support students in interpreting an abstract phrase and shifting from literal word meanings to chapter-level meaning.
Language Focus:
Figurative language interpretation
Contrastive language
Layered interpretation clauses
Name the possible literal interpretation first so students have a clear starting point before moving to the figurative meaning.
Prompt students to explain the mismatch between the phrase and the chapter events because that mismatch is the key to interpretation.
“You said ‘it means fast’—we can explain that by saying ‘the phrase sounds fast on the surface, but the chapter shows progress was being delayed.’”
“That idea connects to figurative language because the official wording hides a slower reality.”
“The phrase literally sounds like ___, but in context it suggests ___.”
“This wording creates tension because ___.”
“The phrase suggests ___, which reinforces the idea that ___.”
Allow students a brief turn-and-talk to clarify ideas, including use of a shared home language, before sharing with the whole group.
If students interpret speed only literally → Prompt: “What do the events show about how long people still had to wait for real change?”
If students name the phrase’s meaning but cannot connect it to central idea → Prompt: “Finish this clause: ‘… which reinforces the idea that progress in the chapter was ___.’”
Student explains both the literal impression and the contextual meaning of the phrase.
Student uses a clause such as “which reinforces the idea that” to move from interpretation to analysis.

Ready for extension
Ask students to explain whether the phrase feels ironic in the chapter and defend their answer with one additional detail.
Invite students to replace “humanity’s first step into the heavens ” with a more direct phrase and discuss how that would change the tone of the chapter.

This part of the lesson helps students identify technical vocabulary and understand how it supports key ideas in the chapter. The 3‑Column Chart guides them to connect specific terms to what they explain and why they matter.
Display the following section of text:

“While the astronauts were preparing for this important mission, Katherine Goble had to calculate the flight trajectories. In other words, she had to plan the exact path that the spacecraft would travel across Earth’s surface, from the moment it lifted off the launch pad and flew through the atmosphere and into space, until it splashed back down in the Atlantic Ocean.” (pg. 150)
Say:

In this passage, the author uses technical vocabulary to explain the complex calculations Katherine had to complete. This explanation helps readers who may not have a scientific background understand challenging concepts. The passage includes words such as
calculate
trajectories
, and
atmosphere
, which help to highlight the key idea that Katherine had to determine the spacecraft’s precise path from launch to landing.

Support students in categorizing evidence into legal progress and scientific progress and explaining how the categories reveal different rates of change.
Language Focus:
Categorizing language
Comparison and contrast connectors
Evidence-based explanation
Prompt students to place every detail in a category and justify why it belongs there.
If students record vague notes, ask them to name the text landmark and what the evidence shows about pace.
“You said ‘this part is about schools’—we can say ‘this detail belongs in delayed legal progress because the chapter shows change was ordered but not quickly carried out.’”
“That idea connects to scientific progress because Project Mercury work moved with urgency and deadlines.”
“This detail belongs in the ___ column because ___.”
“Compared with the school section, the Project Mercury section shows ___.”
“Together, these details suggest that progress was ___.”
Allow students a brief turn-and-talk to clarify ideas, including use of a shared home language, before sharing with the whole group.
If students have trouble sorting vocabulary into legal versus scientific categories → Prompt: “Is this detail about rules and public life or about research and mission work?”
If students list details without explaining pace → Prompt: “Add one word that shows rate: quickly, urgently, slowly, unevenly, or delayed.”
Student correctly sorts details into scientific progress and delayed legal progress.
Student explains the category choice using a connector such as because, however, or compared with.

Ready for extension

Part B: Analyzing the Development of a Central Idea (RI.6.2) (15 minutes)
Quick Write
Teach: Building a Layered Central Idea Explanation
Say:

In Chapter 18, the author uses both figurative and technical language to reveal central ideas. The figurative phrase “the birthplace of humanity’s first step into the heavens” shows Virginia’s pride in its role in early space exploration, while also highlighting the contradiction that the state still enforced segregation and treated Black mathematicians and scientists unfairly. The technical terms—such as calculate, trajectories, and atmosphere—explain the precise, high‑stakes work Katherine was doing at the same time. Together, these language choices show that scientific progress was moving quickly, while social and legal progress lagged behind.
Say these Directions:

Write a four‑to‑five‑sentence explanation of how the figurative phrase “the birthplace of humanity’s first step into the heavens” helps develop a central idea of Chapter 18. Use evidence from the text to support your response.
Display the following writing model if needed for support and guidance:

Chapter 18 shows that progress was not moving at the same speed in every part of American life. The figurative phrase “the birthplace of humanity’s first step into the heavens” presents Virginia as a proud starting point for space exploration; however, the chapter also shows that the state continued to resist integration, treating many of the very people who made that progress possible unfairly. In contrast, the technical language describing Katherine’s calculations highlights how urgent and advanced the scientific work was. This contrast helps reveal a central idea of the chapter, which reinforces the idea that the nation could move rapidly toward space while still delaying justice at home.
Support students in turning categorized evidence into a clear central idea explanation with precise connectors.
Language Focus:
Central idea frames
Causal and contrast connectors
Interpretation clauses
Prompt students to begin with a central idea sentence instead of beginning with a detail.
If students summarize each section separately, ask them to add one sentence that explains the relationship between the two details.
“You said ‘one part is slow and one part is fast’—we can say ‘the chapter presents uneven progress across American life.’”
“That idea connects to central idea because the phrase highlights a contrast, which reinforces the idea that change was not equal in every setting.”
“The central idea of Chapter 18 is ___.”
“In the school section, ___; however, in the Project Mercury section, ___.”
“This contrast matters because it reinforces the idea that ___.”
Allow students a brief turn-and-talk to clarify ideas, including use of a shared home language, before sharing with the whole group.
If students write only about the phrase and leave out chapter evidence → Prompt: “Add one school detail and one Mercury detail to prove your interpretation.”
If students list the two details but do not state a central idea → Prompt: “What bigger idea do both details show about progress?”
Student writes a central idea statement that goes beyond summary.
Student uses a connector and a clause such as “which reinforces the idea that” to explain the relationship between details.
Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Writing a Central Idea Sentence
Provide the frame “Chapter 18 shows that progress was ___ because ___ and ___.”
Struggling with: Connector Precision
Offer a small word bank with however, as a result, therefore, and while, and prompt students to choose the one that best matches their meaning.
Struggling with: Written Expression
Allow students to orally rehearse their response with a partner or use speech-to-text before copying a final draft.
Ready for extension
Ask students to revise their paragraph to include a second interpretation sentence about why the author chose this phrase instead of a more direct one.
Invite students to explain how the phrase connects not only to Chapter 18, but also to earlier unit examples of segregation and delayed recognition.

Part B: Analyzing the Development of a Central Idea (RI.6.2)
Students will write a short explanation connecting figurative language to a central idea in the chapter.
Quick Write
Say these Directions:

In three to four sentences, explain how the author uses both figurative language—such as the phrase “the birthplace of humanity’s first step into the heavens”—and technical language—such as the words calculate, trajectories, and atmosphere used to describe Katherine’s work—to convey central ideas in Chapter 18. Use details from the text to support your response.

The figurative phrase “the birthplace of humanity’s first step into the heavens” shows how proudly Virginia viewed its role in early space exploration. However, the technical terms describing Katherine’s calculations—like calculate and trajectories—highlight the precise, urgent scientific work happening at the same time. Together, these two types of language reveal a central idea of the chapter, which is that scientific progress was advancing quickly even while social progress, such as ending segregation, was being delayed.

standards.description: Interpret figures of speech (e.g., personification) in context.
Use the relationship between particular words (e.g., cause/effect, part/whole, item/category) to better understand each of the words.
Determine a central idea of a text and how it is conveyed through particular details; provide a summary of the text distinct from personal opinions or judgments.
Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings.
Cite textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
By the end of the year, read and comprehend literary nonfiction in the grades 6–8 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.

Come to discussions prepared, having read or studied required material; explicitly draw on that preparation by referring to evidence on the topic, text, or issue to probe and reflect on ideas under discussion.
Produce clear and coherent writing in which the development, organization, and style are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.

Negotiate with or persuade others in conversations using appropriate register (e.g., to reflect on multiple perspectives) using a variety of learned phrases, indirect reported speech (e.g., I heard you say X, and Gabriel just pointed out Y), as well as open responses.

Negotiate with or persuade others in conversations (e.g., to provide counterarguments) using an expanded set of learned phrases (I agree with X, but...), as well as open responses.

Expand noun phrases in simple ways (e.g., adding a sensory adjective to a noun) in order to enrich the meaning of sentences and add details about ideas, people, things, and the like.
